sims.title: What if gravity switched off for 5 seconds?
sims.caption:
What if gravity switched off for 5 seconds? You wouldn't float. The whole planet would spring outward under your feet, and you'd feel nothing until gravity came back. 🌍

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #gravity #studytok #space
sims.science: Earth is in balance between gravity and internal pressure. Remove gravity and every layer (rock, sea, air) accelerates outward at the local g, so the ground keeps pushing on your feet as before. After 5 s: v = 9.81*5 = 49 m/s = 176 km/h, rise = 0.5*9.81*25 = 123 m. Pressure at the centre about 364 GPa = 3.6 million atm. When gravity returns the outward motion continues and the planet oscillates (radial mode period about 20 minutes).

sims.title: Chernobyl, second by second
sims.caption:
Chernobyl, second by second. 36 seconds after the test began, the operators hit the shutdown button, and for a moment it made things worse. This is the physics of why. ☢️

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#chernobyl #simulation #science #physics #radioactivity #history #studytok
sims.science: Test began 01:23:04, AZ-5 pressed 01:23:40 (36 s later), explosions about 01:23:44-48. RBMK: positive void coefficient, graphite-tipped control rods. Power estimated at around 100 times nominal. Upper shield about 1,000 t. I-131 half-life 8 days, Cs-137 30 years. Graphite fire about 10 days.

sims.title: What if the Sun vanished right now?
sims.caption:
What if the Sun vanished right now? For 8 minutes and 20 seconds you'd notice nothing: its last light, and its last gravity, would still be on their way. ☀️

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #space #sun #studytok
sims.science: Sunlight takes about 8 min 20 s to reach Earth (about 150 million km / 299,792 km/s = 499 s). General relativity: changes in gravity travel at the speed of light (GW170817: gravitational waves and gamma rays arrived 1.7 s apart after more than 100 million light-years), so Earth keeps orbiting until the last light arrives, then leaves in a straight line at its orbital speed, 29.78 km/s = 107,000 km/h. Jupiter is 778 million km from the Sun (light time 43 min); seen from Earth it stays lit at least 66-70 min after Earth goes dark (computed from path lengths). Cooling: below freezing within about a week, roughly -100 F (about -73 C, 200 K) within about a year (D. Stevenson, Caltech; Popular Science). Diagram labelled not to scale, time sped up.

sims.title: Titanic, minute by minute
sims.caption:
Titanic, minute by minute. The iceberg didn't rip one huge gash: it opened six thin tears adding up to about a square metre, across one compartment too many. 🚢

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#titanic #simulation #science #history #physics #studytok #whatif
sims.science: 14 April 1912, moonless, unusually calm sea, about 22 knots. Crow's nest bell 11:39 pm ('Iceberg right ahead'), helm hard-a-starboard (ship turns to port), collision about 11:40 pm, under a minute after sighting. Damage: six thin tears, total open area about 1 square metre (12 sq ft), not one gash. 16 watertight compartments; afloat with four flooded; at least five ruptured. Thomas Andrews determined she would founder. Lifeboat 7 left first with about 27-28 people (65 seats). 20 boats, 1,178 places, about 2,200 aboard (53%). About 2:00 am only three collapsibles remained; 2:18 lights out and she broke in two; foundered 2:20 am (2 h 40 min after the collision). About 1,500 died; 705 rescued by the Carpathia (arrived about 3:30 am). Not verified from a page that could be opened in this run, so not stated in the film: the clock times of Andrews's inspection and of the first lifeboat. The cutaway is not to scale; where the hull parts and ice on the deck are illustrative.

sims.title: What if the Earth stopped spinning for one second?
sims.caption:
What if the Earth stopped spinning for one second? The ground would stop, but you, the air and the sea would keep going east at 1,670 km/h. You never feel speed, only a change in speed. 🌍

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #earth #studytok #space
sims.science: Idealised: only the solid planet stops; air, sea and anything loose keep their eastward speed. Equator speed = 2*pi*6378.137 km / 86164.1 s = 465.1 m/s = 1,674 km/h (said as 1,670). Distance in 1 s = 465 m. Speed scales with cos(latitude): 60 deg -> 837 km/h (shown as about 840), poles 0. Escape velocity 11.186 km/s = 40,270 km/h, about 24 times the equator speed, so nothing is thrown into space. Speed of sound 343 m/s = 1,235 km/h at 20 C, from the standard formula 331.3*sqrt(1+T/273.15); the web check of this one figure was blocked in the run, the other figures were checked against the sources below.

sims.title: What if you stepped into space without a suit?
sims.caption:
What if you stepped into space without a suit? You wouldn't explode or freeze solid. You'd have about 10 seconds awake, and around 90 seconds to be rescued. 🧑‍🚀

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #space #astronaut #studytok
sims.science: Sudden exposure to vacuum. Useful consciousness about 10 s (sources give 9-12 s and 10-15 s). Never hold the breath: air in the lungs expands and can rupture them. Water boils at body temperature (37 C) below 47 mmHg = 6.27 kPa, the Armstrong limit (about 63,000 ft = 19.2 km); Jim LeBlanc, whose suit lost pressure in a NASA vacuum chamber, reported the saliva on his tongue bubbling before he passed out (three sources give 1966, one 1965; unconscious in about 14-15 s; recovered with no lasting harm). Body swells to perhaps twice its normal volume (2x volume = 1.26x linear, as drawn); skin holds, no explosion. No instant freezing: no medium to conduct heat; computed radiative loss 0.98*5.67e-8*1.8 m2*306 K^4 = about 880 W, which cools a 70 kg body by about 0.2 C a minute at most. Recompression within about 60-90 s usually allows survival (animal experiments and accidents); death likely after about 2 minutes. Not stated in the film because sources disagree: whether blood itself boils. Station and Earth are not to scale; the 10 s are shown in slow motion.

sims.title: Hindenburg, second by second
sims.caption:
Hindenburg, second by second. The whole airship burned in about 34 seconds, yet 62 of the 97 people on board survived, because hydrogen flames go up. 🔥

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#hindenburg #simulation #science #history #chemistry #hydrogen #studytok
sims.science: 6 May 1937, Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey; left Frankfurt 3 May; landing delayed by thunderstorms (about half a day late). LZ 129, 245 m (803.8 ft) long, 16 hydrogen gas cells. Mooring lines dropped at 7:21 pm from 295 ft = 90 m (two sources; one says about 180 ft, so the film says 'about 90 m'). Fire at 7:25 pm near the tail; witnesses differ on the exact spot (most: ahead of the upper fin), and the film says so. Destroyed in 32, 34 or 37 s depending on the account ('about 34'); the stern dropped and the bow rose before coming down. 97 aboard (36 passengers, 61 crew): 35 died (13 passengers, 22 crew) plus 1 ground crew = 36; 62 survived (97 - 35). Hydrogen burns upward and fast, which made the fire more survivable; many jumped or ran clear. Cause shown as 'most likely, never proven for certain': leaking hydrogen ignited by an electrostatic spark; the US inquiry stated only a mixture of free hydrogen and air, and neither inquiry endorsed sabotage. Not stated because not verified from a page that could be opened in this run: the hydrogen volume, and the helium export law. The film is a simplified reconstruction: the fire's spread, the ship's height and the people on the field are illustrative.

sims.title: What if you fell through a tunnel to the other side of the Earth?
sims.caption:
What if you fell through a tunnel to the other side of the Earth? You'd be weightless the whole way, fastest at the centre where gravity is zero, and you'd arrive in about 38 minutes. 🌍

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #gravity #earth #studytok
sims.science: Idealised: a straight, airless, frictionless tunnel from pole to pole (so the Earth's spin does not matter). In free fall you feel no weight the whole way. Fall time worked out by integrating the PREM density model numerically in this run: 38.0 minutes pole to pole (published: 38 min 11 s with PREM against 42 min 12 s for a uniform-density Earth; Klotz, Am. J. Phys. 83, 231, 2015); the film says 38 minutes. Gravity does not fall steadily: in PREM it stays between 100% and 109% of its surface value down to the core-mantle boundary at 2,890 km (45% of the way to the centre, reached after about 12.7 min), then falls to zero at the centre, where the pull is equal in every direction. Top speed at the centre: the PREM integration gives 9.9 km/s (about 35,700 km/h); the uniform-density textbook value is sqrt(gR) = 7.9 km/s (28,460 km/h); Klotz's paper says 'near 8 km/s' and Live Science quotes 'over 8 kilometers per second'. Because these differ, the film says only 'over 28,000 km/h', which is true in every case. You arrive at the far side with zero speed and fall back unless you hold on. Tunnel length shown as 'about 12,700 km' (diameter about 12,740 km; radius 6,370-6,371 km). Deepest hole ever drilled: Kola Superdeep Borehole, 12,262 m (1989), about 180 C at the bottom; 12.262/6371 = 0.19%, shown as 0.2% of the way to the centre. HUD depths and gravity percentages come from the same PREM integration. Layer names in the film change at 35 km (crust, illustrative), 2,890 km (outer core, liquid iron) and 5,150 km (inner core, solid iron); the 5,150 km figure is the PREM model value and was not confirmed from a page that could be opened in this run, and no figure for it is stated in the film. The tunnel is imaginary (heat and pressure make it impossible to build) and the film says no one can dig it. Cutaway is not to scale (tunnel and crust drawn thicker than they are); time is sped up, with slow motion through the centre; the half-turn that lets you leave head first is illustrative.

sims.title: Apollo 13, second by second
sims.caption:
Apollo 13, second by second. A routine request to stir the oxygen tanks set off the explosion 93 seconds later, 320,000 km from Earth. The lander that never landed kept all three alive. 🚀

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#apollo13 #simulation #science #history #space #nasa #studytok
sims.science: Times are ground elapsed time (GET) from NASA's detailed chronology of the accident. Launch 11 April 1970, 19:13 UT (1:13 pm CST). 55:52:58 Capcom Jack Lousma: '13, we've got one more item for you, when you get a chance. We'd like you to stir up the cryo tanks.' 55:53:18 oxygen tank 1 fans on; 55:53:20 oxygen tank 2 fans on, with electrical disturbances from 55:53:20 to 55:53:41; tank 2 pressure rises, reaching its maximum of 1,008.3 psia at 55:54:45; 55:54:53 the 'bang', telemetry lost for about 2 seconds; 55:55:20 Swigert: 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.'; 55:55:35 Lovell: 'Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a main B bus undervolt.' Fans on to bang: 55:54:53 - 55:53:20 = 93 s (arithmetic run). 55:52:00 GET = 10:05 pm EST 13 April, so the bang was about 9:08 pm in Houston (CST), as NASA's mission page says. Distance: NASA gives 'about 200,000 miles from Earth' = 321,869 km, said as 'three hundred and twenty thousand kilometres' and shown as 'about 320,000 km'. Cause (NASA mission page, review board findings): heater thermostatic switches not upgraded from 28 to 65 volts were probably welded shut during a ground test, wiring near the heaters reached about 1,000 F, which severely degrades Teflon insulation; the film says 'damaged wires spark' and 'the insulation starts to burn' and shows no temperature. Tank 2 blew up 'causing the No. 1 tank to also fail'; two of three fuel cells were lost, and losing all oxygen meant the last fuel cell would die. Lunar module Aquarius: 'designed to support two men for two days' and asked 'to care for three men for about four days'. Splashdown 17 April 1970 in the Pacific; mission duration 5 days 22 h 54 min 41 s. Crew: James Lovell, Jack Swigert, Fred Haise. The chronology does not say which crew member operated the fan switch, so the film says only 'the fans switch on'. Not to scale and labelled so: Earth and Moon sizes and distances; the tank is drawn as a cutaway about 1.5 m wide for clarity; the spark, flame and gas cloud are illustrative; the mission clock on screen runs faster or slower than real time between the verified time marks. The lunar module was cast off before re-entry; the last shot of it alone is illustrative.

sims.title: What if you could see radiation?
sims.caption:
What if you could see radiation? The first thing glowing would be you: around 7,000 atoms decay inside your body every second, and they always have. ☢️

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #radiation #chemistry #studytok
sims.science: Each flash stands for radioactive decays (ionising radiation); visible light is not what is meant. Human body (Health Physics Society, 70 kg adult): potassium-40 about 4,200 Bq (the same page also says 'about 5,000 Bq') and carbon-14 about 3,080 Bq; 4,200 + 3,080 = 7,280, said as 'around seven thousand' decays a second, and the HUD rounds carbon-14 to 'about 3,100'. Banana: 'about 15 Bq of K-40' (Ionactive); the banana is drawn at the true rate (14 sparks on a cycle of about one second), everything else is marked 'not to scale' because thousands of flashes a second cannot be drawn. Smoke alarm: 'one microcurie or less of americium-241' (US NRC); 1 microcurie = 3.7e10 x 1e-6 = 37,000 Bq by definition, said as 'up to thirty seven thousand'. Alpha particles 'only travel a few inches' and the source is sealed in foil and ceramic that stops them leaving the detector (NRC, EPA); the film says 'a few centimetres' and draws a 4 cm ring. Cosmic rays: about 1 muon per square centimetre per minute at sea level (HyperPhysics); 'roughly one or two pass through a hand each second' (Live Science; 100 cm2 x 1/60 = 1.7 a second). The six hand hits in the close-up are drawn at that rate; the wide shots say 'not every one is drawn'. 'You've been radioactive since before you were born' follows from potassium and carbon being part of every living cell. The idea's planned line about granite benchtops was dropped: no granite figure could be confirmed from a page that opened in this run, so the film does not mention granite. No dose figure is stated; the closing line 'what matters is the dose' is the general principle.

sims.title: What if a teaspoon of neutron star appeared on your desk?
sims.caption:
What if a teaspoon of neutron star appeared on your desk? It wouldn't crash through the floor. Without the star's gravity squeezing it, it would burst apart. 💥

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #neutronstar #space #studytok
sims.science: Neutron star: NASA (Imagine the Universe) describes 'an object with the mass of a sun squished down to the size of a city', 'about 20 kilometers (12.5 miles) across', and says 'one sugar cube of neutron star material would weigh about 1 trillion kilograms (or 1 billion tons) on Earth', about as much as a mountain. Astronomy magazine (answer by Valerie Mikles) gives the remnant as 'about 1.5 times the Sun's mass' and a tablespoon as 'more than 1 billion tons (900 billion kg)'. Arithmetic run: 1.4 solar masses (2.78e30 kg) in a 12 km radius sphere (7.24e12 m3) is a mean density of about 3.8e17 kg/m3, so a 5 mL teaspoon is about 1.9e12 kg, roughly 2 billion tonnes; NASA's sugar-cube figure scaled to 5 mL gives about 5 billion tonnes. Sources differ, so the film says only 'billions of tonnes' and 'as much as a mountain'. What happens: the same Astronomy answer says the matter is that dense only because of the star's gravity; brought to Earth, 'what's inside expands very rapidly' and it 'would cause a giant explosion, and it would probably vaporize a good chunk of our planet'. The film says 'a giant explosion, big enough to vaporise part of the planet' and gives no energy figure, because none could be verified from an official source (a comparison with the dinosaur-killing asteroid was dropped for that reason). Free neutron: Particle Data Group mean life 878.3 +/- 0.4 s = 14 min 38 s (shown on the clock, said as 'about fifteen minutes'); decay to proton + electron + antineutrino, about 100 percent. The idea's planned point ('it would blow apart') survived checking. Illustrative and labelled so: the blast over the town and on the globe ('Illustration, not to scale', slow motion, no timing shown); the city beside the star is at the same scale but its buildings are enlarged; the 'bursts in' countdown is a film device, not a measured time; pulsar beams and star surface are stylised; particle sizes in the decay shot are not to scale.

sims.title: What if the Moon disappeared tonight?
sims.caption:
What if the Moon disappeared tonight? The tides wouldn't stop. They'd shrink to less than half, because the Sun pulls on the oceans too. 🌙

Follow for a new simulation every day.

#whatif #simulation #science #physics #moon #tides #studytok
sims.science: Sun's share of the tide: NASA Ocean Motion says 'the sun's tidal pull on the ocean is less than half (about 46%) of the moon's tidal pull'; New World Encyclopedia (Tide) gives theoretical amplitudes of about 54 cm for the Moon and 25 cm for the Sun (46%). Arithmetic run: tidal force goes as mass / distance cubed, so Sun/Moon = (1.989e30 / 7.342e22) x (3.844e8 / 1.496e11)^3 = 0.46. So with the Moon gone the tide-raising pull is 46% of the Moon's alone ('less than half', as the film says) and about a third of today's spring-tide pull (0.46 / 1.46 = 0.32); the film says only 'less than half'. Timing: NASA Ocean Motion gives the lunar day as about 24 h 50 min and says 'the times of high and low tide change by about 50 minutes from one solar day to the next'; a Sun-only tide repeats on the 24-hour solar day, so high tide comes at the same clock times every day (the time-lapse is labelled 'Simple model, real coasts lag'). Light delay: Royal Museums Greenwich gives the average Earth-Moon distance as 384,400 km and 'about 1.3 seconds for light to travel from the Moon'; arithmetic run: 3.844e8 m / 299,792,458 m/s = 1.28 s. Orbit: Earth circles the Earth-Moon centre of mass at about 12 m/s against an orbital speed of 29.8 km/s (0.04%), so 'almost exactly as before'. Tilt: Laskar, Joutel and Robutel (Nature 361, 1993, 'Stabilization of the Earth's obliquity by the Moon') found the tilt varies only about 1.3 degrees around 23.3 with the Moon and could become chaotic without it; Lissauer, Barnes and Chambers (Icarus 217, 2011) found much smaller swings (about 10 degrees), so the film says the tilt 'could start to wander' and labels the shot an illustration with a question mark. The idea's planned point (tides shrink, they do not stop) survived checking. Illustrative and labelled so: the 1.3 s countdown is shown in slow motion; the ocean bulge is 'hugely exaggerated'; orbit and tide diagrams are not to scale; the Moon in the harbour sky is drawn larger than life; the tide height in the harbour is stylised.
